paragraphs: Predicting missing links in a knowledge graph requires models to reason about entities and the different relationships connecting them. Although graph neural networks are widely used for this purpose, their capabilities are less clearly understood than they are for simple graphs. This paper develops a systematic account of what different knowledge-graph models can express when performing link prediction.

The central tool is a relational version of the Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm. The authors use it to characterize the expressive power of different models, bringing apparently unrelated approaches into a shared framework and identifying additional models. They also extend this analysis into logic, precisely describing the class of functions captured by a particular class of graph neural networks.

The contribution is therefore both a way to compare models and an explanation of architectural choices. The theory explains benefits of some design decisions already common in practice, and experiments validate those benefits. This connects formal distinctions in model expressiveness with choices that matter in practical link prediction.
neurips-2023-a-theory-of-link-prediction.tldr: A relational Weisfeiler-Leman framework characterizes knowledge-graph link predictors and explains benefits of practical design choices.

paragraphs: Ridge regression requires choosing a regularization strength that controls how strongly its coefficients are penalized. Leave-one-out cross-validation is one way to make this choice, but its risk can have several poor local minima for finite datasets. Searching a chosen list of candidate strengths can therefore miss good solutions. This paper develops a Bayesian alternative that learns the strength and regression coefficients together.

The method uses an iterative expectation-maximization procedure. Under relatively mild conditions and with enough observations, the authors prove that the Bayesian posterior has a single mode and that their method finds a unique optimum. The guarantee depends on those conditions and the sample size; it is not stated for every finite dataset.

After suitable preprocessing, each main iteration costs O(min(n, p)) operations, versus O(n min(n, p)) for evaluating one regularization value with fast cross-validation. The resulting coefficient estimates match or exceed the quality of cross-validation estimates, particularly with sparse covariates. The approach thus combines cheaper tuning steps with a conditional guarantee that avoids competing local optima.
neurips-2023-bayes-beats-cross-validatio.tldr: A Bayesian expectation-maximization method tunes ridge regression efficiently, with a unique optimum under stated large-sample conditions.

paragraphs: Forecasting a building's near-term energy consumption is useful for power systems, but studying models that transfer across buildings requires diverse training data. BuildingsBench addresses a shortage of large, open datasets with two resources: simulated energy data for 900,000 buildings representing the U.S. building stock, and an evaluation platform covering more than 1,900 real buildings from seven open datasets.

The benchmark separates two ways of transferring knowledge. In zero-shot forecasting, a pretrained model predicts consumption for an unseen building without further training. In transfer learning, the model is fine-tuned using data from the target building. These tasks make it possible to examine both direct generalization from simulation and the value of adapting a pretrained model.

The analysis finds that synthetic pretraining transfers surprisingly well to real commercial buildings. Increasing training-data size and diversity follows a power-law relationship with diminishing returns for zero-shot commercial performance. Fine-tuning improves forecasts for a majority of evaluated commercial and residential buildings. These findings support studying simulation-based pretraining while preserving the distinction between commercial zero-shot results and broader fine-tuning results.
neurips-2023-buildingsbench-a-large-scal.tldr: BuildingsBench provides large-scale simulated training data and real-building evaluations showing promising transfer for energy forecasting.

paragraphs: Many image models expect a fixed set of input channels, such as the three channels in an RGB image. Microscopy does not always fit that arrangement: instruments and experimental goals can change both the number and type of channels collected. Models tied to one channel configuration can consequently be difficult to reuse across studies.

CHAMMI provides a benchmark for investigating models that adapt to these changes. It combines a curated dataset of single-cell images with varying channel counts and an evaluation framework built around biologically relevant tasks. The authors also adapt several existing techniques into channel-adaptive models and compare them with models that use fixed channel configurations.

The findings show that channel-adaptive models can generalize better to tasks outside their original domain and can be computationally efficient. These are demonstrated possibilities rather than a claim that every adaptive design is superior. By supplying both data and an evaluation API, CHAMMI gives future work a common basis for comparing whether flexibility in image inputs translates into useful biological predictions.
neurips-2023-chammi-a-benchmark-for-chan.tldr: CHAMMI benchmarks microscopy models that adapt to varying image channels and shows potential benefits for generalization and efficiency.

paragraphs: Remote-sensing images must support analysis across broad geographic areas and different viewing scales. Hardware constraints and misalignment between images at different scales make learning useful representations challenging. Cross-Scale MAE addresses this problem through self-supervised pretraining, building on a masked autoencoder while making scale variation an explicit part of the learning process.

During pretraining, the method applies scale augmentation and asks representations to remain consistent across scales. It enforces that consistency through both contrastive and generative losses. Together, these objectives guide the model toward representations that agree across scale changes while retaining information useful for reconstruction and subsequent image-understanding tasks.

The implementation also uses xFormers to accelerate pretraining on a single GPU while preserving the quality of learned representations. Experimental evaluations report better performance than standard MAE and other leading masked-autoencoder methods for remote sensing. The contribution combines a learning objective tailored to multiscale imagery with a more efficient implementation, showing that explicit attention to scale during pretraining can improve the representations obtained in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2023-cross-scale-mae-a-tale-of-m.tldr: Cross-Scale MAE improves remote-sensing representations by combining scale augmentation with contrastive and generative consistency objectives.

paragraphs: Active learning in regression asks which measurements are most useful to acquire. Standard formulations often treat each observation as the target function's value at a single point. CS4ML broadens this setup to include Fourier measurements, vector-valued information such as gradients, measurements along continuous curves, and combinations of different measurement types. This is especially relevant when generating scientific data is expensive.

The framework uses random sampling governed by a finite collection of sampling measures and accommodates arbitrary nonlinear model classes. Its central mathematical tool is a generalized Christoffel function, which is used to improve those sampling measures. In practical terms, the framework connects the choice of where or how to measure with the approximation problem being solved.

The authors prove near-optimal sample complexity in several important cases, rather than for every possible measurement and model combination. They demonstrate the framework on polynomial learning with gradient information, MRI using generative models, and adaptive sampling for physics-informed neural networks solving partial differential equations. These applications illustrate how one sampling framework can address substantially different forms of scientific observation.
neurips-2023-cs4ml-a-general-framework-f.tldr: CS4ML uses generalized Christoffel functions to guide active sampling across diverse measurement types, with near-optimal sample complexity in important cases.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization must make decisions under uncertainty, including uncertainty about whether the data distribution will change. Distributionally robust optimization addresses this by accounting for alternative distributions. Earlier work connected these ideas, but practical obstacles remained, including assumptions that contextual variables take only finitely many values. This paper seeks a computationally tractable formulation that also accommodates continuous contexts.

The authors describe distribution shifts using phi-divergences, a family that includes chi-squared divergence, total variation, and Kullback-Leibler divergence. This provides a common treatment of several ways to specify distributional uncertainty. The key result shows that the resulting robust Bayesian optimization problem is equivalent to a finite-dimensional optimization problem, even when the context itself is continuous.

That equivalence makes the method implementable without requiring a finite context set. The authors also prove sublinear regret bounds, providing a formal guarantee on how accumulated decision loss grows. Experiments report improvements over existing methods. The contribution therefore pairs a broader mathematical treatment of distribution shift with a tractable algorithm and both theoretical and empirical support.
neurips-2023-distributionally-robust-bay.tldr: A finite-dimensional reformulation makes distributionally robust Bayesian optimization tractable across phi-divergences, including with continuous contexts.

paragraphs: Learning-curve extrapolation predicts a model's later performance from its early training results. Because many futures can fit the same early observations, the paper argues for predicting a distribution of outcomes. It introduces LC-PFN, a transformer pretrained to approximate Bayesian inference in one forward pass, avoiding repeated expensive inference for each new learning curve.

LC-PFN learns from 10 million artificial curves generated from a parametric prior. These curves are right-censored, meaning their later portions are unobserved in the extrapolation task. The authors report that LC-PFN approximates the posterior predictive distribution more accurately than the compared MCMC approach while running more than 10,000 times faster.

The same model also performs competitively on 20,000 real learning curves spanning four benchmarks, multiple neural architectures, and 53 datasets with different input modalities. In model-selection experiments, a simple predictive early-stopping rule based on LC-PFN produces two- to six-fold speedups on 45 datasets with virtually no overhead. These results connect fast uncertainty-aware extrapolation to a concrete use: deciding when further model training is unlikely to be worthwhile.
neurips-2023-efficient-bayesian-learning.tldr: LC-PFN predicts learning-curve futures with fast approximate Bayesian inference and enables substantial early-stopping speedups in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Knowledge tracing predicts whether a student will answer an exercise correctly to track their knowledge over time. Transformer approaches perform well, but their input features are often chosen manually. The paper also identifies a weakness in relying on a single global context mechanism to capture forgetting, particularly when relevant records are temporally distant from the current interaction.

The proposed approach adds convolutional operations to strengthen local context modeling and uses evolutionary architecture search to choose how local and global processing are combined. Within the search space, a Transformer's attention path becomes the sum of a global path and a local path that may use different convolutions. Input-feature selection is part of the same search.

An evolutionary algorithm explores these alternatives, while a search-space reduction strategy aims to accelerate convergence. The resulting architecture is evaluated on two datasets described as the largest and most challenging in education. The reported results support its effectiveness, showing the value of jointly searching feature choices and the balance between local and global context rather than fixing those decisions manually.
neurips-2023-evolutionary-neural-archite.tldr: Evolutionary search jointly selects input features and local/global processing operations for Transformer-based knowledge tracing.

paragraphs: Action-constrained reinforcement learning requires an agent's action to satisfy constraints at each step. A common solution projects policy outputs into the feasible region by solving an optimization problem. That extra optimization can slow training and convergence, and can create zero gradients that interfere with learning. FlowPG replaces this step with a learned transformation.

The transformation is a normalizing flow: an invertible, differentiable mapping between feasible actions and the support of a simple latent distribution. Training it requires examples of feasible actions, which can themselves be difficult to obtain. The authors develop sampling methods based on Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and probabilistic sentential decision diagrams for convex and non-convex constraints, then integrate the flow with DDPG.

The intended validity property depends on having a well-trained flow, which maps policy outputs into valid actions without an optimization solver. Across evaluated continuous-control tasks, FlowPG produces significantly fewer constraint violations and runs multiple times faster. Several instances show up to an order-of-magnitude reduction in violations. The results support the learned mapping as a practical way to reduce the cost of enforcing action constraints.
neurips-2023-flowpg-action-constrained-p.tldr: FlowPG uses a learned normalizing flow to generate constrained actions efficiently, reducing violations and runtime in continuous-control experiments.

paragraphs: Making graph convolutional networks deeper often produces little improvement and can even hurt performance. Motivated by the usefulness of shallow graph models, this paper introduces graph convolutional kernel machines. These combine kernel functions with graph convolution, providing another way to incorporate graph structure into machine learning without extensive neural architecture design.

A concrete example is a graph convolutional kernel support vector machine for node classification. The authors analyze its generalization error bound and examine how graph structure affects that analysis. The broader framework is described as composable, extendable to large datasets, and applicable to tasks including classification, clustering, feature extraction, and dimensionality reduction.

The paper presents globally optimal solutions, interpretability, and reduced effort in tuning and optimization as advantages over graph convolutional networks. Benchmark experiments find accuracy that is at least competitive with those networks. The findings make the framework relevant when a graph-learning task can benefit from a simpler optimization setup while still using neighborhood information. They do not establish that increasing neural-network depth is unhelpful for every graph task.
neurips-2023-graph-convolutional-kernel-.tldr: Graph convolutional kernel machines combine graph structure with kernel methods, offering competitive accuracy and globally optimal solutions.

paragraphs: Privacy in location data does not always require concealing every approximate indication of where someone is. In some settings, the sensitive information is their precise location. This paper studies Euclidean clustering under distance-based privacy, motivated by that distinction. Its aim is to form useful clusters while protecting location information at the precision relevant to an attacker.

The authors provide algorithms for both k-means and k-median clustering. Their guarantees combine a constant-factor approximation with an additive error term. The important feature of that additional error is that it depends only on the attacker's precision bound, rho, rather than the radius, Lambda, of the entire space. This ties that part of the accuracy guarantee to the privacy requirement's spatial precision.

Experiments find significantly better performance than previous differentially private clustering algorithms and naive distance-based private alternatives. The theoretical and empirical contributions reinforce one another: the guarantees identify a more targeted source of additive error, while the experiments show practical clustering benefits under the studied privacy formulation.
neurips-2023-k-means-clustering-with-dis.tldr: Distance-based private clustering achieves constant-factor guarantees with additive error tied to attacker precision rather than the space's radius.

paragraphs: This paper turns time-series forecasting into text continuation by expressing numerical observations as strings of digits. Under this formulation, a language model predicts future numbers through next-token prediction. The authors find that GPT-3 and LLaMA-2 can forecast without task-specific training at levels comparable to, or better than, purpose-built models trained on the downstream tasks.

Making the approach effective requires careful numerical tokenization and a way to convert discrete token probabilities into densities over continuous values. The authors argue that language models' ability to represent multiple possible outcomes, together with preferences for simplicity and repetition, suits recurring time-series structure. They also demonstrate using text to represent missing observations, supply additional information, and ask questions about predictions.

Larger models generally perform better in the reported work, but the relationship has exceptions. GPT-4 can underperform GPT-3 because of numerical tokenization and poorly calibrated uncertainty. The authors suggest that alignment interventions such as RLHF likely contribute to the calibration issue. This qualification shows why language-model forecasting quality depends on more than model size.
neurips-2023-large-language-models-are-z.tldr: Language models can forecast numerical time series zero-shot, though tokenization and uncertainty calibration strongly affect performance.

paragraphs: Diffusion models have broad distribution-learning capabilities if accurate score estimation is available. That premise leaves an important question unresolved: when can practical gradient-based training actually learn the required quantities? This paper studies that question for Gaussian mixture models and proves efficient recovery of their true parameters by gradient descent on the denoising diffusion probabilistic model objective.

The guarantees cover two specific settings. For a mixture of two spherical Gaussians in d dimensions, random initialization succeeds when the centers have inverse-polynomial separation in d. For a mixture of K spherical Gaussians, the result instead requires a warm start and center separation of order at least the square root of log(min(K, d)). Initialization and separation are therefore essential parts of the statements.

A central proof ingredient connects score-based learning with expectation-maximization and spectral methods, two other approaches to learning distributions. These connections help establish when the diffusion training objective can support efficient parameter recovery. The contribution makes progress from assuming score estimation is possible to proving that a concrete training algorithm succeeds for specified mixture families.
neurips-2023-learning-mixtures-of-gaussi.tldr: Gradient descent on the DDPM objective provably recovers spherical Gaussian mixtures under specified initialization and separation conditions.

paragraphs: Training theory often assumes learning rates are extremely small, even though larger rates produce distinctive behavior in practice. One such behavior is the edge of stability, also described as unstable convergence. This paper investigates that regime through a detailed analysis of gradient descent in simplified two-layer neural networks, aiming to explain a possible benefit of larger training steps.

For these models, the authors prove that edge-of-stability behavior occurs. They also identify a sharp transition in step size: below a threshold, the network fails to learn threshold-like neurons, defined here as neurons with nonzero first-layer bias. The finding links the optimization step size to the kind of features the network can learn.

Threshold neurons provide useful inductive biases for many tasks, so gaining access to them offers one possible explanation for improved generalization near the edge of stability. The conclusion is deliberately narrower than a universal claim about large learning rates. It establishes a mechanism within the analyzed models and shows how training dynamics can influence the building blocks available to the learned predictor.
neurips-2023-learning-threshold-neurons-.tldr: Analysis of simplified networks identifies a step-size transition that connects edge-of-stability training with learning threshold-like neurons.

paragraphs: Interactive decision making includes problems in which an algorithm must learn while choosing actions, such as structured bandits and reinforcement learning. The Decision-Estimation Coefficient measures statistical difficulty in these settings. Earlier work used it both to lower-bound the best achievable regret and to express upper bounds for an approach called Estimation-to-Decisions.

Estimation-to-Decisions converts supervised online estimation algorithms into decision-making algorithms. This paper combines that reduction with a specialized optimistic form of estimation. The resulting analysis permits more lenient notions of estimation error, improving on the earlier guarantees. The key change is therefore in the estimation requirements that can support a rigorous decision-making guarantee.

The authors use this approach to derive regret bounds for model-free reinforcement learning with value-function approximation. They also establish structural results identifying when the optimistic approach can help and when it cannot. This makes the contribution more than a single bound: it clarifies the reach of a general reduction and shows how weaker estimation requirements can support learning good decisions in specified settings.
neurips-2023-model-free-reinforcement-le.tldr: Optimistic estimation strengthens Estimation-to-Decisions guarantees and yields regret bounds for model-free reinforcement learning with value-function approximation.

paragraphs: MotionGPT explores whether human movement and written language can be handled within one language-modeling framework. Its motivation is that motion carries semantic structure, much like body language. A shared model could therefore learn relationships between descriptions and movement while supporting several motion tasks through the same underlying representation.

The method first uses discrete vector quantization to convert 3D motion into motion tokens. These tokens form a motion vocabulary that can be modeled alongside text tokens. MotionGPT is pretrained on a mixture of motion-language data, then fine-tuned on question-and-answer tasks expressed through prompts. This gives different requests a common interface while preserving a representation for the motion itself.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across multiple tasks, including generating motion from text, describing motion, predicting future motion, and filling motion between supplied portions. These results support treating motion as a tokenized language for joint modeling. The contribution is the combination of a discrete motion representation, shared text-and-motion training, and prompt-based task handling within one model.
neurips-2023-motiongpt-human-motion-as-a.tldr: MotionGPT tokenizes 3D movement and models it alongside text to support multiple motion generation and understanding tasks.

paragraphs: Generalized category discovery asks a model to cluster unlabeled images, including images from categories absent from the labeled examples. The paper identifies an ambiguity in common benchmarks: with only one accepted grouping, strong performance may reflect unsupervised clustering rather than learning which categorization the labels specify. That makes it difficult to assess whether models use supervision as intended.

The proposed Clevr-4 dataset has four equally valid groupings based on shape, texture, color, or object count. Labeled examples determine which grouping the model should extend to the unlabeled images. Strong unsupervised models fail on this benchmark, demonstrating that discovering a natural grouping alone is insufficient when several competing taxonomies are valid.

The authors use Clevr-4 to diagnose weaknesses in existing methods and develop a Mean Teacher-based approach called muGCD. It substantially outperforms the implemented baselines on Clevr-4 and achieves a new best result on the real-image Semantic Shift Benchmark suite. The findings connect a more discriminating benchmark with improvements that also transfer to real category-discovery tasks.
neurips-2023-no-representation-rules-the.tldr: Clevr-4 tests whether category discovery follows labeled taxonomies, and the resulting muGCD method improves synthetic and real-data results.

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning builds a binary classifier from a small set of labeled positive examples and many examples whose class is unknown. Some existing methods assume that observed positive labels were selected entirely at random. In real applications, particular positive examples may be more likely to receive labels, producing selection bias that undermines that assumption.

PUe addresses this issue using causal-inference techniques. It reconstructs the training loss with normalized propensity scores and normalized inverse probability weighting, accounting for differences in labeling probability. The paper presents this correction as producing a consistent, unbiased classifier estimate. It also proposes a regularization-based way to estimate propensity scores in deep learning when the labeling mechanism is unknown.

Experiments on three benchmark datasets show significant accuracy improvements over advanced cost-sensitive positive-unlabeled methods when labels are distributed nonuniformly. The findings highlight the importance of modeling how labels become available, in addition to learning how features relate to classes. PUe's contribution combines a correction to the learning objective with a method for estimating the labeling probabilities that correction requires.
neurips-2023-pue-biased-positive-unlabel.tldr: PUe corrects selection bias in positive-unlabeled learning through propensity-based loss weighting and improves accuracy with nonuniform labels.

paragraphs: Image segmentation requests can arrive as words, points, boxes, scribbles, or existing masks. SEEM aims to handle these different forms of instruction through one interactive model. Its decoder places diverse prompts within a common interface, allowing a user to specify what to segment in more than one way and to combine those instructions.

A unified visual prompt represents spatial queries and can extend to a separate referring image. Text and visual prompts share a learned visual-semantic space, enabling their composition. Learnable memory prompts retain segmentation history through mask-guided attention to image features. A text encoder also represents queries and mask labels in the same semantic space to support open-vocabulary segmentation.

The empirical study reports generalization to unseen user intents and competitive results on interactive, generic, referring, and video object segmentation across nine datasets using one set of weights. The abstract also reports supervision as low as one hundredth. The central finding is that shared prompt representations and interaction memory can support diverse segmentation behaviors within a single model.
neurips-2023-segment-everything-everywhe.tldr: SEEM combines visual prompts, text, and interaction memory in one model for diverse segmentation tasks.

paragraphs: Hybrid sequence models combine state-space models with attention, but often apply their attention modules uniformly to every input element. Sparse Modular Activation changes that allocation of computation. It lets a network dynamically choose which submodules each element uses, while keeping the selection differentiable. Elements skip inactive modules, reducing computation and memory use during both training and inference.

The authors instantiate this mechanism in SeqBoat. A state-space model produces representations that guide sparse activation of a Gated Attention Unit. That unit applies local attention only among activated inputs. Under this constraint, SeqBoat achieves linear inference complexity while retaining a theoretically unbounded attention span, and the paper reports a better quality-efficiency trade-off than chunking-based models.

Experiments cover long-sequence modeling, speech classification, and language modeling. SeqBoat achieves new best results among the evaluated class of hybrid models with linear complexity. Its learned activation patterns also reveal how much attention different tasks use. The results support making attention deployment adaptive to the sequence instead of treating its computational cost as uniform across all elements.
neurips-2023-sparse-modular-activation-f.tldr: Sparse Modular Activation lets SeqBoat selectively apply attention, improving efficiency while achieving strong results among linear-complexity hybrid models.

paragraphs: Sparse linear models are interpretable because they base predictions on a limited set of features with explicit coefficients. Their simplicity also restricts flexibility. The contextual lasso addresses a setting in which inputs divide into explanatory features, whose effects should be interpretable, and contextual features, which determine which explanatory variables matter and how strongly they contribute.

The method fits a linear model in the explanatory features, but allows both its selected variables and coefficients to change with context. A deep neural network learns this dependence without prescribing a fixed parametric form. A projection layer maps the network's output into the space of linear models satisfying an l1 constraint, providing the lasso-style regularization needed for sparse coefficients.

Experiments on real and synthetic data suggest that the resulting models can be sparser than ordinary lasso while retaining the predictive power of a standard deep network. The interpretation is local to the chosen context: the active explanatory variables and their effects remain explicit, while the neural network supplies flexibility in how those effects vary.
neurips-2023-the-contextual-lasso-sparse.tldr: The contextual lasso uses a neural network to choose context-dependent sparse linear coefficients, combining flexibility with explicit feature effects.

paragraphs: Robotic learning can involve several simultaneous requirements, such as avoiding collisions, conserving energy, and maintaining balance. Handling only average costs may be insufficient when failures matter. This paper introduces the safe distributional actor-critic, or SDAC, a trust-region-based reinforcement-learning algorithm designed to handle multiple constraints with a risk-averse treatment of their outcomes.

SDAC contributes two mechanisms. A gradient integration method addresses infeasibility issues that arise in problems with several constraints and comes with a theoretical convergence result. A TD(lambda) target distribution supports estimation of risk-averse constraints with low bias. Together, these mechanisms address both how to update the policy and how to estimate the risks those updates should respect.

The evaluation covers robotic tasks with multiple constraints and with a single constraint. Relative to safe reinforcement-learning baselines, the paper reports 1.93 times fewer steps to satisfy all constraints in the former and 1.78 times fewer violations in the latter, while maintaining high scores. These findings show improved constraint handling in the tested tasks alongside strong task performance.
neurips-2023-trust-region-based-safe-dis.tldr: SDAC combines multi-constraint policy updates with distributional risk estimation to improve constraint satisfaction in robotic reinforcement-learning experiments.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning makes exploration difficult because the shared state space can be large and agents influence one another. Sparse task rewards further reduce guidance. The authors observe that different exploration strategies help in different scenarios, motivating a framework that combines curiosity about unfamiliar outcomes with attention to how one agent affects others.

COIN implements these two signals in different parts of learning. It measures each agent's influence on other agents using mutual information and applies the resulting intrinsic reward to individual value functions. Separately, it derives curiosity rewards from prediction errors and adds them to the external task reward. A shared framework integrates the two sources of exploratory motivation.

The proposed combination is intended to make curiosity and influence complementary: one encourages investigating poorly predicted experiences, while the other accounts for interactions within the team. Experiments across challenging benchmarks report superior performance in different scenarios. The contribution is a simple integration of two exploration signals, supported by the finding that the usefulness of each kind of exploration varies across cooperative tasks.
neurips-2023-two-heads-are-better-than-o.tldr: COIN combines prediction-error curiosity with mutual-information-based influence rewards to improve exploration in cooperative multi-agent learning.

paragraphs: Off-policy learning to rank improves a ranking system using interaction data collected by a previously deployed system. A difficulty is that observed clicks depend on how users respond to the displayed ranking. Existing approaches often assume a particular click-generation model, requiring their learning procedures to be redesigned when those assumptions change.

This paper formulates ranking under general stochastic click models as a Markov decision process. That reformulation makes it possible to learn the optimal ranking directly through offline reinforcement learning. The resulting method, CUOLR, uses a dedicated decision-process formulation to adapt across a wide range of click models without requiring prior knowledge of the click model or complex debiasing procedures.

Experiments on several large-scale datasets report that CUOLR consistently outperforms leading off-policy ranking algorithms while remaining consistent and robust across different click models. The contribution is a common learning formulation for settings that previously called for specialized methods. Its findings support using offline reinforcement-learning tools to connect logged user behavior with ranking improvement across the studied click-generation settings.
neurips-2023-unified-off-policy-learning.tldr: CUOLR formulates ranking as an offline reinforcement-learning problem that adapts across click models without prior knowledge of their form.
